"Men have gaped at me with their mouth" (16:10); Not being able to see God. "Behold, he passes by me, and I see him not" (9:11). "If I summoned him and he answered me, I would not believe that he was listening to my voice" (9:16); A wish not to have been born. "Why did you bring me out from the womb?" (10:18). "leave me alone, that I may find a little cheer" (10:20); Hope beyond the anger, in the same breath. "Oh that you would hide me in Sheol, that you would conceal me until your wrath be past, that you would appoint me a set time, and remember me! … You would call, and I would answer you; you would long for the work of your hands" (14:13, 15). Job asks for a hiding place from God's anger in God's own keeping, and expects God to long for him afterwards.

Part 2 verses: what they add. Three new strands: (a) The eye wasting, as in Job 17:7; "My eye wastes away because of grief; it grows weak because of all my foes" (Psa 6:7), after "every night I flood my bed with tears" (6:6); "My eye is wasted from grief; my soul and my body also. For my life is spent with sorrow" (Psa 31:9–10); The eye is where ka'as shows in the body, in all three texts (Job 17:7; Psa 6:7; 31:9); What turns Psa 6 round is being heard: "the Lord has heard the sound of my weeping. The Lord has heard my plea" (6:8–9). In Psa 10:14, "you do see, for you note mischief and vexation, that you may take it into your hands; to you the helpless commits himself". The vexation is seen by God, and the helpless hands it over; (b) Provocation from those closest; "A foolish son is a grief to his father and bitterness to her who bore him" (Pro 17:25); The reverse direction: "Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger" (Eph 6:4), and "do not provoke your children, lest they become discouraged" (Col 3:21); Vexation passes both ways between parent and child. Col 3:21 names its outcome as losing heart. Hannah's rival (1Sa 1:6) was a co-wife. These are the family members; (c) Qoheleth's vexation: the vexation of the thinker and the worker; Knowing brings it: "in much wisdom is much vexation, and he who increases knowledge increases sorrow" (Ecc 1:18). This comes after "I applied my heart to know wisdom … this also is but a striving after wind" (1:17); Work brings it, and it keeps the heart awake: "his work is a vexation. Even in the night his heart does not rest" (2:23); "all his days he eats in darkness in much vexation and sickness and anger" (5:17); Its answer is enjoyment received as God's gift: "There is nothing better … than that he should eat and drink and find enjoyment in his toil. This also, I saw, is from the hand of God" (2:24), and "this is the gift of God" (5:19); It is to be removed: "Remove vexation from your heart, and put away pain from your body" (11:10), after "Rejoice, O young man … let your heart cheer you" (11:9); It is sometimes better than laughter: "Sorrow [ka'as] is better than laughter, for by sadness of face the heart is made glad" (7:3). The one place where ka'as is valued. The face is sad and the heart made good. Face and heart go in opposite directions.

Primary Hebrew term is baqash (H1245), root meaning 'to seek, require, desire, exact, request' -- showing an active volitional pursuit rather than passive reception.

The full vocabulary arc for baqash runs from mundane request (Esth.2.15, asking for nothing), through intellectual/existential search (Eccl.8.17), relational-devotional pursuit (Ps.27.8, Isa.65.1), to violent pursuit of a life (Jer.11.21, 37.7 context, 38.16, 44.30) -- showing the term's range covers virtually all objects of human desire and pursuit, benign to hostile.

M16 (wise, H2450) and M15 (know, H3045) and M23 (cannot, H3201) co-occur but describe the futility of human search for wisdom, not a direct functional relation to seeking itself; seeking here is the frustrated activity, wisdom/knowing are its unattained objects.
The toiling man initiates the seeking, directed toward the hidden 'work of God' as its object, but the verse asserts the pursuit fails to reach its target.

Numbers 17:5: "Thus I will make to cease from me the grumblings of the people of Israel": The verse closes a long dispute over who God has chosen. It begins in Numbers 16. Korah and 250 chiefs, *"chosen from the assembly, well-known men"* (16:2; *qārîʾ*, H7148, "called"), rise up: *"Why then do you exalt yourselves above the assembly of the Lord?"* (16:3). Moses answers with God's choosing: *"The one whom he chooses he will bring near to him"* (16:5), and *"the man whom the Lord chooses shall be the holy one"* (16:7).; Moses names what is underneath the complaint: *"is it too small a thing for you that the God of Israel has separated you … And would you seek the priesthood also?"* (16:9–10). What they already have is not enough. They seek more.; *"Therefore it is against the Lord that you and all your company have gathered together. What is Aaron that you grumble against him?"* (16:11). The grumbling at Aaron is against the Lord.; Psalm 106 names the same event with an inner word: *"When men in the camp were jealous of Moses and Aaron, the holy one of the Lord, the earth opened and swallowed up Dathan, and covered the company of Abiram"* (Psa 106:16–17).; Moses himself is *"very angry"* (16:15). The rebels are judged (16:31–35). The next day *"all the congregation of the people of Israel grumbled against Moses and against Aaron, saying, 'You have killed the people of the Lord'"* (16:41). A plague begins, and Aaron *"stood between the dead and the living, and the plague was stopped"* (16:48).; Then God settles it with the staffs: *"And the staff of the man whom I choose shall sprout. Thus I will make to cease from me the grumblings of the people of Israel, which they grumble against you"* (17:5). The grumbling is against Moses and Aaron, and God calls it *"from me"*. In v10 it is *"their grumblings against me"*. The staff is kept *"as a sign for the rebels, that you may make an end of their grumblings against me, lest they die"* (17:10).; The grumbling turns to terror: *"Behold, we perish, we are undone, we are all undone. Everyone who comes near … shall die. Are we all to perish?"* (17:12–13).; "Grumble" is *lûn* (H3885B). The verse shows it as spoken complaint. I read the inner side from the passage: the seeking of the priesthood (16:10), and the jealousy that Psalm 106:16 names.

What others do around a choice, in these verses: grumble against the chosen man, and God counts it as against himself (Num 16:11; 17:5, 10); seek more than they were given, and are jealous (Num 16:10; Psa 106:16); name a choice as shame, and are angry at what it costs them (1Sa 20:30–31); despise the chosen in the heart, by the eyes of people (2Sa 6:16, 20); despise and abhor the chosen servant (Isa 49:7); conclude from the chosen people's ruin that God rejected them, and despise them in their own sight (Jer 33:24); ask to share the joy of the chosen (Psa 106:5); not know God, and still be called and equipped for the sake of the chosen (Isa 45:4–5); offer an inner act, the humbling of the soul, that God's choosing weighs and does not accept (Isa 58:3–5)

Grumbling, and seeking more. When God's choice of Aaron was challenged, Moses named what lay under it: *"would you seek the priesthood also?"* (Num 16:10). The grumbling at Aaron was against God: *"What is Aaron that you grumble against him?"* (16:11), and God calls it *"the grumblings … which they grumble against you"*, to be made to *"cease from me"* (17:5). Then the grumbling became terror: *"Are we all to perish?"* (Num 17:13).

The full range shows the term operates identically whether the object sought is a person, God, material need, or protection -- always denoting active, purposeful pursuit.

The characteristic is 'Seeking/Inquiring' (H1875 darash), a term signaling formal, careful consultation or resort to — often used of seeking God through worship/prayer, or of a ruler/judge exacting requirement.

At the definitional level darash means to resort to, frequent, consult, inquire of, seek deity in prayer/worship, seek with a demand/requirement, investigate, or study/follow with application — showing a term straddling cultic devotion and legal/administrative demand.

The name carries a strong constitutional implication in covenant contexts: to darash the Lord is to constitute or maintain the relationship of dependence and consultation; failure to do so (1Chr 10:14) constitutes covenant breach leading to death and transfer of kingship.

The vocabulary distinguishes disposition versus act: darash names ongoing habitual seeking (participial 'one who seeks justice', Isa 16:5) versus punctual failure-to-seek as a completed act (1Chr 10:14, Qal perfect).

1Chr 10:14 itself supplies the structural opposite in narrative form: 'he did not seek [darash] the Lord' — the negated form functions as the vocabulary's own antonym-in-context, i.e. covenant neglect/abandonment.

Hos 10:12's 'seek the Lord' and 1Chr 10:14's negated 'did not seek the Lord' both sit within darash's standard covenantal-seeking sense; no notable divergence beyond polarity (positive command vs. negative narrative report).

In 1Chr 10:14, no other M-code characteristic besides M83 (seeking, negated) is present; the verse reports Saul's failure to seek the Lord as the sole characterized quality driving the narrative consequence (death, transfer of kingdom).
In 1Chr 10:14, the (negated) seeking operation would have been initiated by Saul (party) toward the Lord (party, T7); its absence is the operative narrative fact leading to his death.

The characteristic's presence marks a person as rightly oriented toward God in covenant fidelity, and its absence marks corruption or apostasy (Ps.10.4, 1Chr.10.14 'He did not seek guidance from the Lord... the Lord put him to death'); this indicates that the capacity to seek/inquire is part of humanity's created relational orientation toward God, and its exercise or neglect functions as a diagnostic marker of the divine image's proper functioning or its corruption in the person.

Where seeking is present in a person (2Chr.22.9 'sought the Lord with all his heart'), it indicates the divine image is functioning rightly in relational orientation toward God; where absent (Ps.10.4, 1Chr.10.14), it indicates a corrupted or suppressed image-bearing capacity, evidenced by pride and covenant unfaithfulness leading to death.

The structural opposite of seeking is forsaking/neglecting -- explicitly named as the contrastive pole in 1Chr.28.9 ('if you forsake him, he will cast you off forever') and implied by negation in Ps.10.4 ('does not seek') and 1Chr.10.14 ('did not seek guidance') -- the inner-being reality that excludes seeking is self-sufficient neglect or active abandonment of the source that ought to be consulted.

Grammatical range is verbal only (Qal and Niphal), appearing as finite verbs, infinitives, and participles across these verses -- showing the characteristic operates as an action performed by an agent, never as an abstract noun-state in this strong.

In Jer.10.21 and 1Chr.15.13 'inquire'/'seek' align with the standard cultic-consultation sense of H1875 (consulting the Lord), with no notable divergence from the base gloss.

H1245 (baqash) at the definitional level denotes seeking to find, seeking to secure, seeking someone's face, desiring/demanding, requiring/exacting, and asking/requesting -- a verb of active pursuit with both benign (devotional seeking) and forceful (demanding, requiring) senses.

The name carries a directional implication: seeking is always oriented TOWARD an object or person (a face, a person, a deity, an answer, a due) -- it structurally implies a subject in motion toward a goal not yet possessed, whether that goal is relational (seeking the Lord) or transactional (requiring blood, demanding an allowance).

Primary Hebrew term H1245 baqash; root sense of active searching-out, whether for a lost/absent object (Song 5.6), for divine favour/presence (1Chr 16.10; Ps 105.3), for words/oracles (Isa 45.19), or for accountability (require blood, Ezek 33.8; demand allowance, Neh 5.18).

H1245 is exclusively verbal (Piel/Pual), occurring as perfect, imperative, participle, and imperfect forms across this batch -- showing the characteristic operates as an ACTION performed by an agent, not a static noun-quality; it is realized only in the doing of seeking.
No dedicated person-type noun ('seeker') appears among these occurrences; the participle form in 1Chr 16.10/Ps 105.3 functions substantivally ('those who seek') but is not a distinct lexeme.

H1245 itself functions as the supplication/seeking term in these verses (seeking the Lord in 1Chr 16.10 and Ps 105.3) -- the root names the very act of seeking from another (here, seeking divine favour/presence).

Across its occurrences here the vocabulary arc runs from intimate personal loss-and-search (Song 5.6), through prophetic critique of futile seeking (Isa 45.19), devotional seeking of Yahweh (1Chr 16.10; Ps 105.3), to juridical exaction (Ezek 33.8 blood-requiring; Neh 5.18 demanding provisions) -- showing the root covers the full range from relational yearning to formal legal claim.
In Song 5.6, 1Chr 16.10, Ps 105.3, and Isa 45.19 the surface gloss 'sought/seek/Seek' sits squarely within the base sense of active searching/desiring with no notable divergence.
No other M-code characteristic is tagged in Ps.105.3 alongside H1245's seeking of the Lord.
In 1Chr.16.10 and Ps.105.3, H1245 (seek) is an operation initiated by worshippers ('those who seek'), directed toward the Lord as its object.

Darash at the definitional level shows resorting/treading to a place, consulting (especially of God or oracular figures), and seeking with care or application -- a term that spans physical approach and mental/spiritual inquiry.
Primary Hebrew term is darash (H1875); root meaning shows a physical sense of treading/resorting to a place that extends metaphorically to consulting, inquiring of, or worshipfully seeking a deity.

Semantic range spans: resorting to a place, consulting God or mediums, worshipful seeking in prayer, demanding/requiring, investigating, studying/practicing with application, and caring for. Idiomatically 'seek the face' denotes seeking audience/favor.

No structural opposite term (e.g. 'forsaking' or 'neglecting') appears within this word group itself; darash's negation is expressed periphrastically elsewhere, not by a dedicated antonym lexeme in these verses.
Darash itself functions as the supplication/seeking term -- the act of seeking God's presence or favor, as in 1Chr.16.11 and Ps.105.4's imperative 'seek his presence continually.'
No NT-period coinage applies to this OT Hebrew term; it is an established pre-existing Hebrew root.
In 1Chr.16.11/Ps.105.4 'Seek [the Lord]...seek his presence' sits squarely within the devotional-consultative base sense; no divergence.

In 1Chr.16.11/Ps.105.4, darash ('seek') co-occurs with M83's own H1245 (baqash, also 'seek') and M23 (H5797, strength). The two seeking-verbs together intensify the plea: seeking the Lord's strength AND presence are portrayed as parallel, mutually reinforcing acts of devotion rather than distinct characteristics competing for attention.

The 'Seek' surface form in this pass (Amos.5.4/5.6/5.14, 1Chr.16.11, Ps.105.4, Isa.55.6, Isa.34.16) is used almost exclusively in imperative form as an urgent devotional/covenantal exhortation ('Seek the LORD/his strength/good and live') rather than as narrative report of consultation -- a distinct sub-mode of this subgroup's formal-inquiry sense: exhortation to habitual, life-orienting seeking of God rather than a single act of consulting an oracle for a specific verdict.

1Chr.22.19 'seek the Lord' is the classic devotional sense (1a3a), squarely within the base gloss.

In 1Chr.22.19, darash (seek the Lord) sits alongside M47 (heart/mind, 'set your mind and heart to seek') and M44 (covenant, the ark of the covenant) -- the seeking here is explicitly heart-directed, showing darash functions as the outward enactment of an inward disposition (heart/mind) toward covenant faithfulness.

In 1Chr.22.19 and 2Chr.15.12 seeking is framed as a settled, wholehearted disposition ('set your mind and heart to seek', 'seek the Lord... with all their heart and with all their soul') rather than a transient emotional reaction -- the language of heart/soul signals an internalized, durable orientation.

The felt quality of seeking varies by context: it is crisis-driven and emotionally anguished in Ps.77.2 and 2Chr.20.3 (trouble, fear), yet presented as a settled, wholehearted covenantal disposition in 1Chr.22.19, 2Chr.15.12, and 2Chr.22.9 ('sought the Lord with all his heart') -- the same term covers both transient emotional response and durable devotional orientation depending on narrative occasion.

Seeking takes hold rightly under conditions of wholeheartedness and sincerity: 'set your mind and heart to seek' (1Chr.22.19), 'with all their heart and with all their soul' (2Chr.15.12), and freedom from co-present idolatry -- in Ezek.14.7 the presence of idols in the heart is what disqualifies otherwise-outward consultation. Genuine seeking requires an undivided heart free from rival objects of devotion.

The evidence shows seeking engages the heart/soul level most deeply and consistently ('with all their heart and with all their soul', 2Chr.15.12; 'set your mind and heart', 1Chr.22.19), with the body's role limited to expressive gesture (Ps.77.2's stretched-out hand) rather than being the seat of the characteristic itself. The pattern indicates seeking's depth and seat is the heart/soul (volitional-affective center), while the body-link (where present) is expressive/indicative of the inner state rather than mediating or generative of it -- darash never engages purely bodily/instinctive levels without heart involvement in these texts.

The pattern of engagement shows heart/soul faculties (mind, will, affection) consistently engaged when seeking is genuine (1Chr.22.19 'set your mind and heart', 2Chr.15.12 'with all their heart and with all their soul'), while purely external/ritual engagement without heart involvement is exposed as illegitimate (Ezek.14.3-7) -- indicating the characteristic's nature is fundamentally a volitional-relational act requiring the engagement of the inner faculties, not a mechanical or merely verbal performance.

Adjacent characteristics appearing alongside seeking include 'heart/mind' (M47, frequently paired as the seat/manner of seeking, e.g. 1Chr.22.19, 2Chr.15.12, Ps.119.2/10), 'trust' (M19, Ps.9.10, Isa.31.1), and 'forsake' (M30/M59, as antithetical pairing, Ps.9.10, 1Chr.28.9) -- these co-occur with notable frequency, showing seeking is characteristically bound to heart-language and its antithesis, forsaking.

Seeking is a constituent element of the larger characteristic of 'setting the heart' (2Chr.19.3, 2Chr.30.19, 1Chr.22.19 all pair 'set the heart/mind' with 'to seek') -- the heart-setting act supplies the internal disposition of which seeking is the outward-directed enactment, making seeking a component within the fuller act of wholehearted devotion.

Setting the heart to seek (cf. Batch B §0.1): "set your mind and heart [*heart and soul*] to seek the Lord" (1Ch 22:19); "those who had set their hearts to seek the Lord" (2Ch 11:16); "you … have set your heart to seek God" (2Ch 19:3); "who sets his heart to seek God … even though not according to the sanctuary's rules" (2Ch 30:19); "Ezra had set his heart to study [*seek*] the Law" (Ezr 7:10); Failure: "he did evil, for he did not set his heart to seek the Lord" (2Ch 12:14)

The vocabulary distinguishes disposition versus act within its own semantic tree: sense 1a3 'to seek deity in prayer and worship' (a disposition of devotion) versus 1a2 'to consult, enquire of' (a discrete act of oracular consultation), and 1b1 'to allow oneself to be enquired of' marks the received/passive side reciprocal to the human given/active side.

No structural-opposite term for H1875 itself is present in these verses; H5800A 'forsake' (a separate strong) functions as the contextual antonym in 1Chr.28.9 and Isa.58.2 but is not part of H1875's own vocabulary set.

In Isa.58.2, Ezra.6.21, and 1Chr.28.9 'seek/worship' sits squarely within the base cultic-consultation/devotion sense of H1875, with no further distinguishing nuance beyond ordinary devotional seeking of God.

M15 (know), M36 (serve), M34 (whole/forever), M47 (heart/mind), M64 (plan), M06 (thought), M30/M59 (forsake), M18 (willing) all co-occur with H1875 in 1Chr.28.9; H1875's own vantage is that the verse pairs two mirrored uses of darash -- human seeking of God and divine searching of the heart -- forming the verse's relational spine that the other M-codes (serving, willing heart, forsaking) orbit as conditions or consequences of that mutual seeking.

God's extension of the characteristic (his willingness to be sought/found) is shown as both conditional and responsive: conditional on genuine seeking ('If you seek him, he will be found by you, but if you forsake him, he will cast you off forever', 1Chr.28.9), yet also shown as gracious and unconditioned in Isa.65.1 ('I was ready to be sought by those who did not ask for me') -- God's self-disclosure as available to be inquired of exceeds strict conditionality, showing both a covenantal-conditional pattern and a gracious-responsive pattern.

Adjacent characteristics appearing alongside seeking include 'heart/mind' (M47, frequently paired as the seat/manner of seeking, e.g. 1Chr.22.19, 2Chr.15.12, Ps.119.2/10), 'trust' (M19, Ps.9.10, Isa.31.1), and 'forsake' (M30/M59, as antithetical pairing, Ps.9.10, 1Chr.28.9) -- these co-occur with notable frequency, showing seeking is characteristically bound to heart-language and its antithesis, forsaking.

Seeking consistently PRECEDES finding/being found and its resulting blessings: Jer.29.13 'You will seek me and find me'; Isa.55.6 'Seek the Lord while he may be found'; 1Chr.28.9 'If you seek him, he will be found by you' -- the sequence is invariably seek-then-find, never the reverse, establishing seeking as the necessary antecedent condition.

The seek-then-find sequence is causal-conditional rather than merely correlational or developmental: the finding is explicitly conditioned upon the seeking ('IF you seek him, he WILL be found'), establishing a covenantal cause-and-effect relationship rather than a coincidental temporal succession.

section_heading: The heart is hidden, and God sees it

obs_text: H1245 (baqash) is this cluster's home term for 'seeking' -- the programme names it as the disposition/act of actively pursuing something desired or required, including seeking God, seeking help, or seeking sustenance. Its essential nature is directed pursuit, not passive hope.

H1245 at the definitional level denotes active seeking-to-find or seeking-to-secure, including seeking a person's face, demanding, requesting; the Piel stem intensifies the pursuit as deliberate effort rather than chance encounter.

H1245 occurs as a verb across Piel active participle (seeking, ongoing action, Isa.41.17, Exod.33.7), Piel perfect (completed seeking, Hos.7.10, Lam.1.19), and Pual passive (seek/be sought, 2Chr.7.14) -- showing the characteristic operates primarily as an ongoing or repeated action rather than a static state.

H1245's semantic range spans physical seeking (water, food -- Isa.41.17, Lam.1.19), covenantal/cultic seeking (seeking the LORD at the tent of meeting, seeking his face -- Exod.33.7, 2Chr.7.14), and idiomatic non-return (Hos.7.10, negated seeking as covenant failure); it can combine with 'face' (H6440) idiomatically to mean seek audience/favor with someone.

No distinct vocabulary within H1245's own forms differentiates disposition-versus-act or received-versus-given; the Piel/Pual distinction is grammatical voice (active seeking vs being sought), not a disposition/act split.

H1245 itself functions as the supplication/seeking term for this cluster -- the act of seeking something (including God) from another is precisely its core sense, most explicit in 2Chr.7.14's seeking God's face as a penitential act.

As an OT Hebrew term, H1245 establishes seeking-God as covenantal practice (tent of meeting, temple prayer); this pattern anticipates NT-period seeking language (e.g. Greek zeteo) that carries forward the same directed-pursuit sense toward God -- continuity of concept across Testaments, though this cluster's own NT term is not covered by these front-loaded strongs.

In 2Chr.7.14 'seek my face' is the classic idiomatic combination (seek + face) meaning seeking God's favor/presence in penitence -- squarely within the base gloss's known idiomatic use, no further divergence.

In 2Chr.7.14, seeking (H1245, seek my face) sits within a tightly-related chain with M09 (humble themselves) and M60 (forgive): seeking is the middle act -- following humbling and preceding turning -- that directs the humbled disposition specifically toward God's face/presence, making it the pivot that connects self-abasement to the divine forgiving response.
In 2Chr.7.14, H1245 is the role-T3 operation: 'my people' (party) initiate the seeking, directed toward God's 'face' (representing the divine party) as part of the penitential sequence.

What goes with it: saying "The Lord is righteous" (2Ch 12:6); tearing clothes, sackcloth, fasting, going about "dejectedly" (1Ki 21:27); weeping (2Ki 22:19); entreating and praying (2Ch 33:12–13); fasting and seeking (Ezr 8:21); the condition "humble themselves, and pray and seek my face and turn from their wicked ways" (2Ch 7:14); confession, and making amends for iniquity (Lev 26:40–41).

'seek' is here the seeking of God: the heart or will turned to him (his face, name, word or help), in its different degrees: wholehearted, in distress, resolved, or negated; the seeking is itself the inner operation.

The primary term's grammatical range in this batch is exclusively verbal (Piel/Pual stem forms: perfect, imperfect, infinitive construct, participle), showing the characteristic operates as an ACTION -- an ongoing or completed act of pursuit -- rather than as a static noun-named quality or disposition.

2Chr.11.16 pairs baqash with 'setting the heart' toward seeking the Lord -- a devotional/covenantal nuance (idiom 'seek the face/God') distinct from the hostile-pursuit and material-search senses seen elsewhere in this batch; here the impact is one of loyal devotion drawing people to Jerusalem.

M47 (heart) co-occurs with baqash in 2Chr.11.16 as the instrument/disposition by which the people direct their seeking toward the Lord; from the seeking-vantage the heart-term supplies the internal resolve preceding the outward act of seeking, a preparatory relation rather than thematic overlap.

In 2Chr.11.16 baqash (role-T3) is initiated by 'those who had set their hearts' and directed toward 'the Lord God of Israel' -- a devotional operation with worshippers as initiators and the Lord as the sought party.

The name carries a strongly relational/directional implication: one goes TOWARD an object of inquiry (God, oracle, person, genealogical record), implying covenantal or investigative orientation rather than static possession.

Semantic range spans resorting to a place, consulting God or idols, seeking deity in worship, demanding/requiring, investigating, and diligent study/practice -- covering physical, cultic, judicial and intellectual seeking.
Darash itself functions as the supplication/seeking term when directed at God (sense 1a3), e.g. 2Chr.15.12's covenant 'to seek the LORD' -- inquiry of deity IS the act of supplication here.

OT darash (cultic/investigative inquiry of God) finds NT continuity in G2212 zeteo's broader seeking/striving sense, though the NT term generalizes beyond the OT's strong cultic-consultation nuance into ordinary human searching and hostile pursuit.

Full vocabulary arc of darash runs from mundane physical resort to a place, through legal/investigative inquiry, to the highest religious sense of seeking God in prayer and worship -- showing the term bridges the physical, judicial, and devotional domains under one root.
2Chr.15.12's 'seek the LORD' represents the term's paradigmatic cultic sense (1a3) -- no divergence from base gloss, this is the central religious usage.

2Chr.15.12 pairs darash (seeking the LORD) with M44 (covenant) and M47 (heart/soul) -- from seeking's vantage, the covenant-act frames the seeking as its formal occasion, while heart/soul specify the wholehearted manner of the seeking; these are complementary but not synonymous with the seeking-action itself.
In 2Chr.15.12 darash ('seek') is the operation, initiated by the covenanting people, directed toward the LORD the God of their fathers -- a party-directed act of covenantal devotion.

In 1Chr.22.19 and 2Chr.15.12 seeking is framed as a settled, wholehearted disposition ('set your mind and heart to seek', 'seek the Lord... with all their heart and with all their soul') rather than a transient emotional reaction -- the language of heart/soul signals an internalized, durable orientation.

Seeking takes hold rightly under conditions of wholeheartedness and sincerity: 'set your mind and heart to seek' (1Chr.22.19), 'with all their heart and with all their soul' (2Chr.15.12), and freedom from co-present idolatry -- in Ezek.14.7 the presence of idols in the heart is what disqualifies otherwise-outward consultation. Genuine seeking requires an undivided heart free from rival objects of devotion.

The characteristic operates differently within an existing covenant bond versus across relational distance: within Israel's covenant with God it is commanded and expected as ongoing devotion (2Chr.15.12, Deut.4.29), whereas toward foreign/false deities or across the covenant boundary it is explicitly forbidden and provokes judgment (Deut.12.30 'do not inquire about their gods'; 2Chr.25.20 'sought the gods of Edom'). The same act of seeking is covenant-faithful or covenant-breaking depending entirely on which relational bond it serves.

The characteristic clearly crosses covenantal boundaries in the evidence -- it is used both of Israel's covenant-faithful inquiry of the Lord (1Kgs.22.8, 2Chr.15.12) and of pagan/foreign inquiry practices (2Kgs.1.2 inquiring of Baal-zebub; Isa.19.3 Egyptians inquiring of idols and mediums), showing darash is not confined to the covenant community's proper object but names the general human act of formal consultation regardless of which deity or authority is addressed.

The evidence shows seeking engages the heart/soul level most deeply and consistently ('with all their heart and with all their soul', 2Chr.15.12; 'set your mind and heart', 1Chr.22.19), with the body's role limited to expressive gesture (Ps.77.2's stretched-out hand) rather than being the seat of the characteristic itself. The pattern indicates seeking's depth and seat is the heart/soul (volitional-affective center), while the body-link (where present) is expressive/indicative of the inner state rather than mediating or generative of it -- darash never engages purely bodily/instinctive levels without heart involvement in these texts.

The pattern of engagement shows heart/soul faculties (mind, will, affection) consistently engaged when seeking is genuine (1Chr.22.19 'set your mind and heart', 2Chr.15.12 'with all their heart and with all their soul'), while purely external/ritual engagement without heart involvement is exposed as illegitimate (Ezek.14.3-7) -- indicating the characteristic's nature is fundamentally a volitional-relational act requiring the engagement of the inner faculties, not a mechanical or merely verbal performance.

The characteristic is primarily an ACT (a verb of deliberate consultation/inquiry performed on an occasion), but recurring wholehearted usages ('seek with all your heart', ongoing 'as long as he sought the Lord') show it can also function as a sustained DISPOSITION -- a settled devotional orientation rather than a single event.

Adjacent characteristics appearing alongside seeking include 'heart/mind' (M47, frequently paired as the seat/manner of seeking, e.g. 1Chr.22.19, 2Chr.15.12, Ps.119.2/10), 'trust' (M19, Ps.9.10, Isa.31.1), and 'forsake' (M30/M59, as antithetical pairing, Ps.9.10, 1Chr.28.9) -- these co-occur with notable frequency, showing seeking is characteristically bound to heart-language and its antithesis, forsaking.

No distinct antonymous lexeme is present in these verses; opposite sense is achieved by simple negation of darash itself (Ps.10.4 'does not seek').

In Ps.10.4 darash (negated: 'does not seek') occupies the negative pole of the cluster's dual seeking-motif, paired with M08 pride and M58 wickedness in the same verse -- the wicked's pride is what suppresses the seeking-act, making darash's absence diagnostic of the wicked disposition.
In Ps.10.4, the seeking operation (negated) is attributed to 'the wicked' (party) with God as its withheld object -- the wicked initiates no such act toward God.

In Ps.10.4 the wicked's failure to seek God reveals his conclusion 'There is no God' -- the absence of inquiry is itself diagnostic of a settled unbelief; the characteristic here reveals a negative judgement about God's non-existence or irrelevance.

Across the verses both patterns occur: seeking/inquiring often precedes a resulting belief or outcome (e.g. 2Chr.14.7 'we have sought the Lord... he has given us peace', Ps.34.4 'I sought the Lord, and he answered me'), while elsewhere the failure or presence of seeking follows from an already-settled disposition (Ps.10.4's pride precedes and explains the non-seeking; 2Chr.12.14's evil is explained by not having set the heart to seek). The characteristic functions bidirectionally as both antecedent to and consequence of belief/judgement.

Seeking is blocked or nullified when the heart harbors idols or a stumbling block of iniquity even while outwardly consulting God -- Ezek.14.3, 14.7 explicitly describe men who 'have taken their idols into their hearts' yet 'come to a prophet to consult me' -- God declares he will not let himself be consulted (or will answer in judgment) in such cases; similarly pride (Ps.10.4 'in the pride of his face') suppresses seeking altogether.

The characteristic's presence marks a person as rightly oriented toward God in covenant fidelity, and its absence marks corruption or apostasy (Ps.10.4, 1Chr.10.14 'He did not seek guidance from the Lord... the Lord put him to death'); this indicates that the capacity to seek/inquire is part of humanity's created relational orientation toward God, and its exercise or neglect functions as a diagnostic marker of the divine image's proper functioning or its corruption in the person.

Where seeking is present in a person (2Chr.22.9 'sought the Lord with all his heart'), it indicates the divine image is functioning rightly in relational orientation toward God; where absent (Ps.10.4, 1Chr.10.14), it indicates a corrupted or suppressed image-bearing capacity, evidenced by pride and covenant unfaithfulness leading to death.

The structural opposite of seeking is forsaking/neglecting -- explicitly named as the contrastive pole in 1Chr.28.9 ('if you forsake him, he will cast you off forever') and implied by negation in Ps.10.4 ('does not seek') and 1Chr.10.14 ('did not seek guidance') -- the inner-being reality that excludes seeking is self-sufficient neglect or active abandonment of the source that ought to be consulted.

At its edge, seeking excludes casual, passive, or half-hearted attention -- it resists mere outward performance without inner devotion (Ezek.14.3-7's idol-hearted consulters are the negative exemplar), and it excludes self-sufficiency/pride that renders inquiry unnecessary (Ps.10.4).
Face of aph (H0639), The face lifted in pride: The face/nose raised (Psa 10:4 ("In the pride of his face the wicked does not seek him")). Pride is the nose held high (S, lexical).

It has no room for God: "In the pride of his face the wicked does not seek him; all his thoughts are, 'There is no God'" (Psa 10:4); "his soul is puffed up; it is not upright within him, but the righteous shall live by his faith" (Hab 2:4). Then: "an arrogant man who is never at rest. His greed is as wide as Sheol" (2:5). The swollen soul is set against faith, and joined to restlessness and greed.
Turns toward help (Deu 33:26): Human pride: Turns away from God: "does not seek him" (Psa 10:4).

'seek' is here the seeking of God: the heart or will turned to him (his face, name, word or help), in its different degrees: wholehearted, in distress, resolved, or negated; the seeking is itself the inner operation.

First pass: darash names the culminating act the Lord looks for -- understanding (M16) is presented as the necessary prior condition/companion of true seeking; the two are paired as a single ideal (one who understands AND seeks God), with darash naming the outward-turned pursuit and M16 the inward comprehension enabling it.

Ps.22.26 'those who seek him' uses darash in its worshipful/devotional sense (seeking God in praise and satisfaction) rather than the oracular-inquiry sense dominant in the Kings narratives -- here the nuance is communal, joyful seeking tied to being satisfied and praising, showing the term's range extending to worship-postures beyond formal consultation.

Ps.22.26 co-occurs darash (seek) with M09 (afflicted), M45 (satisfied), M08/M16/M22 (praise), M47 (hearts), M34 (forever). From inquiring's vantage: seeking the Lord here is the PRECONDITION for the sequence of affliction being resolved into satisfaction and praise -- seeking initiates the chain that other M-codes in this verse then complete (satisfaction, praise, enduring life), rather than being a mere co-occurring quality.
Ps.22.26: the seeking is initiated by 'those who seek him' (the afflicted worshippers, generic party) and directed toward the Lord (T7/T10 party), the object of both seeking and subsequent praise.

The humble seek: "Seek the Lord, all you humble of the land, who do his just commands; seek righteousness; seek humility; perhaps you may be hidden on the day of the anger of the Lord" (Zep 2:3). Those already called humble are told to seek humility. I read: in this verse humility is not a thing held once and for all. The humble keep seeking it, under the threat of the day of anger (2:2); "I will leave in your midst a people humble and lowly. They shall seek refuge in the name of the Lord" (Zep 3:12). They are left after God removes "your proudly exultant ones" (3:11). They are described by what they do and do not do: "they shall do no injustice and speak no lies" (3:13); "The afflicted shall eat and be satisfied; those who seek him shall praise the Lord" (Psa 22:26) and "you who seek God, let your hearts revive" (Psa 69:32). In both, the humble or afflicted stand beside "those who seek". (Psa 22:26 is the afflicted sense, group VI.).

Humble hearts revive: "When the humble see it they will be glad; you who seek God, let your hearts revive" (Psa 69:32); "The afflicted shall eat and be satisfied … May your hearts live forever!" (Psa 22:26).

Baqash is a common pre-NT Hebrew root with no coinage relevance; it is fully attested throughout the OT corpus.

Across the vocabulary arc, H1245 ranges from ordinary seeking (finding, requesting) through consultative seeking (inquiring of God) to hostile seeking (pursuing a life to destroy), showing the term's full range covers both constructive pursuit and destructive intent depending on context and object sought.

In Ps.38.12 those hostile to the psalmist (the party 'those who seek') initiate the seeking-operation, directed toward the psalmist's life/hurt -- an adversarial party seeking harm against the sole party present as target.

baqash's idiom 'seek the life/soul' (e.g. Ps.38.12, 2Sam.4.8, Prov.29.10, Jer.4.30, Jer.11.21) consistently means 'seek to kill', a lethal-hostile-pursuit sense sharply diverging from the term's more neutral or devotional occurrences (e.g. 2Chr.15.13 'seek the Lord'), showing the root's moral valence is entirely determined by its grammatical object.

shachar's semantic range is narrower and more intensively focused than baqash or darash, concentrated almost entirely on 'diligent/early/earnest' seeking -- most frequently of God (Ps.63.1, Isa.26.9, Prov.8.17) but also of prey/food (Job.24.5) or a seductive target (Prov.7.15) -- its moral neutrality (like baqash's) is set by object, but its distinguishing feature vs. the other two Hebrew roots is the added connotation of urgency/priority tied etymologically to 'dawn'.

H7836 (shachar) shares the subgroup's general 'intensive/earnest seeking' theme with G1567/G1934 conceptually (both Greek terms and shachar converge on devotional 'seek God/wisdom diligently' senses: shachar in Ps.63.1, Isa.26.9, Job.8.5, Prov.8.17, Ps.78.34 parallels ekzeteo in Acts.15.17/Heb.11.6/Rom.3.11 and epizeteo's aspirational uses), but there is no lexical or morphological relationship -- shachar is a distinct Hebrew root (tied etymologically to 'dawn/early') with no direct Greek cognate among this subgroup's members, and unlike ekzeteo/epizeteo it never carries a judicial 'demand an account/blood' sense; its 'demanding' pole (Job.7.21, God seeking Job) is ironic-reversal rather than legal exaction.

Unlike both Greek members, whose intensifying force comes from a prefix added to a plainer root (zeteo), shachar's intensifying force is inherent to the lexeme itself (traditionally linked to the noun for 'dawn,' i.e. built-in urgency/earliness rather than compounded prepositional intensification) -- so the subgroup's 'intensive/exhaustive seeking' label is achieved by two different linguistic mechanisms: Greek compounding (ek-/epi- + zeteo) versus a single Hebrew root whose own core meaning already encodes earliness/earnestness.

Where the subgroup's seeking is directed toward God/wisdom, it reveals a belief that the sought one exists, rewards, or can be found (Heb.11.6 'believe that he exists and that he rewards'; Prov.8.17 'those who seek me diligently find me'; Ps.63.1). Where it is directed toward a sign or an account (Matt.12.39/16.4, Luke.11.50-51), it reveals unbelief or a demand for proof/accountability rather than settled belief. In Heb.12.17 Esau's seeking reveals a late realization/perception that what was lost cannot be regained.

In Ps.63.1 the felt quality is intense, bodily, and settled -- 'earnestly I seek you; my soul thirsts...my flesh faints' -- a whole-person longing rather than a passing impulse. In Heb.12.17 it is transient but acute -- 'sought it with tears', a burst of grief-driven desperation. In Matt.16.4 it is a demanding, testing posture rather than an emotion of longing.

The pattern shows the characteristic engaging soul/spirit level pervasively (Ps.63.1 'my soul thirsts,' Isa.26.9 'my spirit within me earnestly seeks') and occasionally the body as an expressive overflow (Ps.63.1 'my flesh faints'), but the body link is expressive/indicative rather than causally central -- the body registers the intensity of the soul/spirit's seeking rather than itself seeking. The characteristic never engages a purely bodily mechanism independent of soul/spirit direction.

Where a body link exists (Ps.63.1's 'flesh faints'), it runs from soul/spirit expressing through the body -- the flesh's fainting is downstream evidence of the soul's thirst, not an independent bodily initiator of the seeking. This means the physical symptom testifies to, rather than generates, the seeking-characteristic.

Where the characteristic operates devotionally (ekzeteo in Heb.11.6, Rom.3.11; epizeteo in Heb.11.14, Heb.13.14; shachar in Ps.63.1, Isa.26.9, Job.8.5, Prov.8.17), the seeker perceives God/wisdom/a homeland as real, attainable, and worth pursuing -- the act presupposes a prior belief that the object exists and rewards the seeker (explicit in Heb.11.6: 'must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him').

The immediate response varies by context and register: it ranges from grief-driven urgency (Heb.12.17, tears), to bodily longing (Ps.63.1, thirst/faint; Isa.26.9, soul yearning), to hostile testing (Matt.16.4, demand for a sign), to calm ongoing pilgrim-orientation (Heb.11.14, Heb.13.14). There is no single uniform immediate response across the subgroup -- it is shaped entirely by whether the seeking is devotional, judicial, or testing.

Yes, the mechanism differs sharply by context. In devotional contexts the mechanism is voluntary, inward pursuit toward God/wisdom (Ps.63.1, Prov.8.17, Heb.11.6). In judicial contexts the mechanism is imposed accountability -- an external divine reckoning exacted from a party regardless of their will (Luke.11.50-51, passive 'will be required'). In testing contexts the mechanism is demand made of another as proof/leverage (Matt.16.4, epizeteo demanding a sign). In physical-need contexts the mechanism is survival-driven foraging (Job.24.5).

The evidence points to both created design and fallen distortion. The created-design pole appears where seeking God is the proper human posture (Heb.11.6, Ps.63.1, Prov.8.17, Acts.15.17) -- an intended capacity oriented toward God as its fulfillment. The fallen-condition pole appears where seeking is either absent altogether (Rom.3.11, 'no one seeks for God') or twisted into hostile demand (Matt.16.4, testing sign-seeking) or exacted judicially against guilt (Luke.11.50-51). The same capacity for intensive seeking is thus shown as originally God-directed but corruptible into either default neglect or adversarial demand.

In devotional occurrences the felt quality is intense and bodily: Ps.63.1 pairs 'earnestly I seek' with 'my soul thirsts... my flesh faints,' and Isa.26.9 pairs it with 'my soul yearns... in the night.' These are not settled dispositions alone but acute, felt longing, expressed through explicit bodily/emotional language (thirst, fainting, yearning at night).

The felt quality varies sharply by context: acute bodily/emotional intensity in devotional seeking (Ps.63.1, Isa.26.9), grief in failed retrospective seeking (Heb.12.17), settled ongoing disposition in pilgrim-seeking (Heb.11.14, Heb.13.14, presented without emotion-language as a simple ongoing orientation), and no stated inner feeling at all in the judicial/demanding occurrences (Luke.11.50-51, Matt.16.4) where the term functions almost mechanically as legal exaction or test.

Yes. The mode varies by direction and context: human-to-God seeking operates inwardly/volitionally (Ps.63.1, Prov.8.17, Heb.11.6); God-to-human/generation operates judicially through passive exaction (Luke.11.50-51, 'will be required'); person-to-person demanding operates confrontationally through speech (Matt.16.4, 'seeks for a sign' addressed to Jesus); person-to-object/need operates through physical activity (Job.24.5, foraging for game). The same lexical family thus spans volitional, judicial, verbal, and physical modes depending on the relational direction.

The human-to-God movement of seeking requires an inner posture of humility, acknowledged need, and expectant faith: Job.8.5 pairs seeking God with pleading for mercy; Heb.11.6 requires prior belief in God's existence and rewarding nature; Ps.63.1 and Isa.26.9 show the posture as one of felt lack (thirst, yearning) reaching toward fulfillment; Prov.8.17 frames the posture as love paired with diligence.

The evidence engages spirit/soul-level seats primarily (Ps.63.1: 'my soul thirsts'; Isa.26.9: 'my spirit within me earnestly seeks') with body given expressive rather than causal role ('my flesh faints for you' as an outward sign of the soul's longing, not a bodily-originated act). The judicial/demand occurrences (Luke.11.50-51, Matt.16.4) engage no inner-constitutional level explicitly, operating instead at the level of corporate/legal accountability. The body link where present is expressive/indicative -- signaling the intensity of soul-level longing -- never the seat or origin of the seeking itself.

In Ps.63.1 the body link runs from soul to body expression: the soul's thirst (inner seeking-longing) is expressed outwardly in the flesh's fainting -- the direction is soul/spirit expressing through the body, not the body generating or feeding back to shape the soul's seeking.

The origin is multiple and changes with context: it originates from divine initiative in judicial contexts (God's demand exacted, Luke.11.50-51), from human volition in devotional contexts (the individual's own choice to seek God, Ps.63.1, Job.8.5), and from collective/corporate disposition in the sign-demanding contexts ('this generation' as a corporate moral agent, Matt.16.4). No single fixed origin holds across all occurrences.

The characteristic consistently engages volitional and affective faculties (will/desire: Ps.63.1's thirst, Prov.8.17's love-paired diligence) and occasionally cognitive faculties (belief, Heb.11.6's 'must believe'), but rarely engages purely rational/discursive faculties in isolation -- even the 'searched and inquired carefully' of 1Pet.1.10 (investigative diligence) is paired with prophetic revelation rather than autonomous reasoning. This pattern indicates the characteristic's nature is fundamentally an act of the whole person's directed will and desire toward an object, not a purely intellectual exercise.

The characteristic is primarily an ACT -- an enacted operation of intensive seeking or demanding, attested grammatically almost exclusively as verbs (active, passive, participial) across all three member strongs, rather than as a noun-form disposition, condition, or quality. Where it recurs habitually (e.g. Heb.13.14's ongoing pilgrim-seeking, or 'this generation' repeatedly demanding a sign) it functions as a repeated act rather than a distinct static disposition-noun.

The characteristic is compound in structure: each member combines a base 'seek' root with an intensifying element -- ekzeteo (ek- 'out/thoroughly' + zeteo), epizeteo (epi- 'upon/toward' + zeteo), and shachar (an inherently intensive root tied etymologically to 'dawn/early,' functioning as a built-in intensifier rather than a compounded prefix). The constituent elements are: (1) the base act of seeking, and (2) an added element of thoroughness, direction, or urgency.

H1245 at the definitional level denotes active seeking-to-find or seeking-to-secure, including seeking a person's face, demanding, requesting; the Piel stem intensifies the pursuit as deliberate effort rather than chance encounter.

The name carries a strongly directional/relational implication: it always assumes an object sought (water, food, God, a person) and implies a relationship of pursuit toward that object, often with the further implication of a response awaited from what is sought.

H1245's Piel root meanings converge on active, applied seeking: to seek to find, to seek to secure, to seek a face, to desire/demand, to require/exact, to ask/request; Pual passive 'to be sought' extends the range to the object's being pursued by another.

H1245 occurs as a verb across Piel active participle (seeking, ongoing action, Isa.41.17, Exod.33.7), Piel perfect (completed seeking, Hos.7.10, Lam.1.19), and Pual passive (seek/be sought, 2Chr.7.14) -- showing the characteristic operates primarily as an ongoing or repeated action rather than a static state.

Numerous M-codes co-occur in Isa.58.2 (M18 delight, M15 know, M76 ways, M12 righteousness/judgment, M21 ask); H1875's own vantage is that 'seeking' functions as the umbrella act framing all these other qualities as its objects/means -- the people seek God's ways, delight, and righteousness together, with H1875 supplying the overarching pursuit-verb that the other M-codes qualify or specify.

Looks right: "they seek me daily and delight to know my ways, as if they were a nation that did righteousness … they delight to draw near to God" (Isa 58:2). The next verse, already in 10.6, is "you seek your own pleasure, and oppress all your workers" (58:3). The delight is real enough to be named twice. I read that delight in religion can sit beside oppression without either one cancelling the other in the person's own eyes.

An inner act weighed by what God chooses: In one passage the inner act of the others is itself set against God's choosing. The people fast and ask, *"Why have we humbled ourselves, and you take no knowledge of it?"* (Isa 58:3). They *"delight to know my ways"* and *"delight to draw near to God"* (58:2). Yet *"in the day of your fast you seek your own pleasure, and oppress all your workers"* (58:3). Then: *"Is such the fast that I choose, a day for a person to humble himself?"* (58:5). "Humble himself" is the humbling of the soul, the same words as their own complaint. What God does choose is turned outward: *"to let the oppressed go free"*, *"to share your bread with the hungry"*, *"not to hide yourself from your own flesh"* (58:6–7).; The self-humbling they offered was not wrong in itself. The passage says it stood beside oppression and quarrelling in the same people, and that it was not what he chooses.

Both Greek terms thus independently develop the same two-pole range (earnest seeking <-> exacting demand) from the same simple root, making them the closest pair in this subgroup.

Where the subgroup's seeking is directed toward God/wisdom, it reveals a belief that the sought one exists, rewards, or can be found (Heb.11.6 'believe that he exists and that he rewards'; Prov.8.17 'those who seek me diligently find me'; Ps.63.1). Where it is directed toward a sign or an account (Matt.12.39/16.4, Luke.11.50-51), it reveals unbelief or a demand for proof/accountability rather than settled belief. In Heb.12.17 Esau's seeking reveals a late realization/perception that what was lost cannot be regained.

Both patterns occur. In devotional occurrences the seeking follows a prior belief (Heb.11.6 -- one must first 'believe that he exists' before seeking him for reward), while in penitential occurrences (Hos.5.15, Ps.78.34) seeking follows judgment/distress and produces or confirms acknowledgment of guilt. In judicial occurrences (Luke.11.50-51) the 'seeking/requiring' itself constitutes the judgement (an act of holding accountable), so it does not precede a separate belief but enacts one.

Frequent co-occurring adjacent characteristics include: faith/belief (Heb.11.6, drawing near to God), understanding (Rom.3.11, paired negatively with seeking), love (Prov.8.17, Prov.13.24), repentance (Hos.5.15, Ps.78.34, Heb.12.17), guilt-acknowledgment (Hos.5.15), and hardening (Rom.11.7). Sign-demanding contexts co-occur with 'evil' and 'adulterous' descriptors of the generation (Matt.12.39, Matt.16.4, Luke.11.29).

A recurring sequence: acknowledgment of guilt precedes seeking (Hos.5.15 'until they acknowledge their guilt and seek my face'); belief precedes seeking (Heb.11.6, 'must believe...and that he rewards those who seek him'); seeking precedes finding (Prov.8.17 'seek me diligently find me'); and being killed/judged precedes repentance which accompanies seeking (Ps.78.34 'When he killed them, they sought him; they repented').

Where the characteristic operates devotionally (ekzeteo in Heb.11.6, Rom.3.11; epizeteo in Heb.11.14, Heb.13.14; shachar in Ps.63.1, Isa.26.9, Job.8.5, Prov.8.17), the seeker perceives God/wisdom/a homeland as real, attainable, and worth pursuing -- the act presupposes a prior belief that the object exists and rewards the seeker (explicit in Heb.11.6: 'must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him').

Across the verses, the characteristic follows a belief more often than it precedes one: Heb.11.6 makes belief in God's existence and rewarding character the explicit precondition for seeking; Hos.5.15 and Ps.78.34 show acknowledgment of guilt/repentance preceding the earnest seeking. In the demanding-sign occurrences, however, the seeking itself reveals an already-formed unbelieving judgment (the generation is 'evil and adulterous') rather than producing a new belief -- so the characteristic mostly follows or expresses prior belief/disposition rather than generating one, with the sign-demanding cases showing seeking as an expression of settled unbelief rather than a step toward belief.

The characteristic takes hold rightly under conditions of faith and acknowledged need: Heb.11.6 requires belief that God exists and rewards seekers as the precondition; Hos.5.15 and Ps.78.34 show acknowledgment of guilt and repentance as the inner condition preceding earnest seeking; Job.8.5's conditional ('if you will seek God and plead...for mercy') ties right operation to humility and plea for mercy rather than self-justification.

The human-to-God movement of seeking requires an inner posture of humility, acknowledged need, and expectant faith: Job.8.5 pairs seeking God with pleading for mercy; Heb.11.6 requires prior belief in God's existence and rewarding nature; Ps.63.1 and Isa.26.9 show the posture as one of felt lack (thirst, yearning) reaching toward fulfillment; Prov.8.17 frames the posture as love paired with diligence.

The human-to-God direction shows a relationship of dependent trust and reward-expectation, not self-sufficiency: the person who seeks believes God exists, rewards seekers (Heb.11.6), and can be found by diligent seekers (Prov.8.17, Jer-style promise pattern) -- the relationship is one where God is approachable and responsive to genuine seeking, contrasted starkly with Rom.3.11's indictment that fallen humanity does not by default seek God at all.

Where seeking is rightly directed toward God as its intended fulfillment (D5.2.3/D11.1.1's created-design pole), it instantiates the divine-image aspect of relational orientation toward God -- the capacity to reach, desire, and pursue communion with one's maker, mirroring (in creaturely form) God's own initiative-taking and pursuing character (cf. God's own seeking of Israel, Hos.5.15's 'I will return... until they... seek my face').

Where the characteristic is present as genuine, faith-grounded pursuit of God (Heb.11.6, Ps.63.1), it indicates the divine image functioning rightly in its relational orientation toward God. Where it is absent entirely (Rom.3.11, universal indictment) it indicates the divine image's relational faculty toward God is disabled/inoperative in fallen humanity apart from grace. Where it is present but distorted into hostile demand (Matt.16.4) it indicates the image's capacity for genuine relational reaching has been turned toward self-justifying testing instead.

God extends the characteristic (or its reward) both conditionally and responsively: Heb.11.6 makes finding God conditional on faith and seeking; Job.8.5 frames restoration as conditional on Job's own seeking and pleading; Hos.5.15 shows God's own withdrawal as conditional and responsive -- he 'returns' precisely when guilt is acknowledged and his face sought, showing the divine response is contingent on the human seeking act rather than unconditional.

God's extension of reward/response to seekers shows a disposition of genuine responsiveness and reward-giving rather than aloofness: he 'rewards those who seek him' (Heb.11.6) and promises 'find me' to diligent seekers (Prov.8.17), and his withdrawal in Hos.5.15 is itself framed as purposeful, aimed at provoking the very seeking that will restore relationship -- disciplinary rather than punitive abandonment.

No occurrence in this subgroup shows the characteristic being communicated, strengthened, or mediated through angelic ministry; all instances of extension or blocking are attributed to God directly, to Christ, to Wisdom personified, or to human agents -- angelic mediation is entirely absent from the evidence.

The characteristic consistently engages volitional and affective faculties (will/desire: Ps.63.1's thirst, Prov.8.17's love-paired diligence) and occasionally cognitive faculties (belief, Heb.11.6's 'must believe'), but rarely engages purely rational/discursive faculties in isolation -- even the 'searched and inquired carefully' of 1Pet.1.10 (investigative diligence) is paired with prophetic revelation rather than autonomous reasoning. This pattern indicates the characteristic's nature is fundamentally an act of the whole person's directed will and desire toward an object, not a purely intellectual exercise.

Adjacent characteristics recur across the subgroup's verses: faith/belief (Heb.11.6, pistis-family), understanding (Rom.3.11, paired negation with G4920), grace/salvation (1Pet.1.10), repentance (Heb.12.17, Hos.5.15, Ps.78.34), love (Prov.8.17, Prov.13.24), guilt-acknowledgment (Hos.5.15), and hardening (Rom.11.7). Faith/belief and repentance are the most frequent co-occurring characteristics, appearing across multiple member strongs.

The co-occurrence pattern shows this characteristic sits at a hinge-point in the inner-being landscape: it regularly pairs with cognitive/relational preconditions (faith, belief, guilt-acknowledgment, repentance) that must be present for it to operate rightly, and with outcome-states (finding/reward, or hardening/failure) that follow from whether it is taken up successfully -- marking intensive seeking as a pivotal, transitional characteristic rather than a self-contained end-state.

obs_text: H1875 (darash) at the definitional level denotes resorting to or frequenting a place, consulting/enquiring of God or false gods, seeking deity in prayer/worship, demanding or requiring, investigating, and studying/practicing with application -- combining cultic consultation with juridical/investigative demand.

Primary Hebrew term H1875 darash; root sense of formally consulting or resorting to (a deity, an oracle, an authority), extending to investigating, demanding, and diligently seeking someone's welfare (as in Esth 10.3's 'sought the welfare of his people').

H1875 appears here as Qal infinitive construct, Qal participle (Esth 10.3, functioning adjectivally/verbally as 'one who sought'), and Niphal imperfect (Ezek 20.3, passive 'be inquired of') -- showing the characteristic operates both as an active verb of consultation and, in the Niphal, as a passive state of being available to be consulted (applied uniquely to God).

The semantic range spans idolatrous oracular consultation (inquiring of Baal-zebub, 2Kgs 1.6, 1.16), refusal of prophetic consultation from a rebellious people (Ezek 20.3, twice -- both the elders' coming to inquire and the Lord's refusal to be inquired of), and a wholly distinct extended/idiomatic sense of diligently seeking someone's good or welfare (Esth 10.3, 'sought the welfare of his people') -- showing the root can shift from cultic-oracular to benevolent-pastoral care.

Across these occurrences the vocabulary arc runs from idolatrous oracular consultation (Baal-zebub, 2Kgs 1.6/1.16), through prophetic refusal of consultation from a rebellious Israel (Ezek 20.3), to a benevolent extension meaning to actively seek someone's welfare (Esth 10.3) -- the full range covers cultic/oracular, prophetic-refusal, and pastoral-care senses under one root.

In Esth 10.3 'sought the welfare of his people' diverges markedly from the base cultic/oracular gloss 'inquire of a deity' -- here darash carries a benevolent-pastoral nuance of actively promoting another's good, with clear impact: it frames Mordecai's greatness in terms of care for his people rather than religious consultation, distinguishing this occurrence from the 2Kgs and Ezekiel occurrences where the oracular sense dominates.

No other M-code characteristic is tagged in Esth.10.3 alongside H1875's seeking of the people's welfare; the adjacent 'welfare' term (H2896B) carries other M-codes but is not this cluster's home strong.
In Esth.10.3, H1875 (sought) is an operation initiated by Mordecai, directed toward the welfare of his people -- a benevolent operation aimed at a collective party's good rather than at a deity.

'sought' is here a desire or purpose of the will directed to an object (glory, wisdom, peace, a sign, rest, favour, one's own good, or a turning to other gods), good or ill; the direction of the will is what 'sought' names.
In Ps.34.4 'I sought the Lord' uses H1875 in its central worship-sense (1a3a, seeking deity in prayer), matching the base gloss with no divergence -- a paradigmatic devotional use of the term.
The psalmist (party, 'I') initiates the seeking operation directed toward the Lord; the Lord in turn answers and delivers, forming a reciprocal operation-chain of seek-answer-deliver.

M45 (delivered) is also present but names the Lord's responsive action after seeking, not an interaction with the seeking-characteristic's own nature; the two are sequential (seek then deliver) rather than mutually defining.

Across the verses both patterns occur: seeking/inquiring often precedes a resulting belief or outcome (e.g. 2Chr.14.7 'we have sought the Lord... he has given us peace', Ps.34.4 'I sought the Lord, and he answered me'), while elsewhere the failure or presence of seeking follows from an already-settled disposition (Ps.10.4's pride precedes and explains the non-seeking; 2Chr.12.14's evil is explained by not having set the heart to seek). The characteristic functions bidirectionally as both antecedent to and consequence of belief/judgement.

The immediate response to seeking is varied across contexts: it produces answer/deliverance (Ps.34.4), peace (2Chr.14.7), prospering (2Chr.26.5), being found (Jer.29.13), but also, when directed at illegitimate objects, provokes divine anger (2Chr.25.15) or judgment ('come to nothing', Amos.5.5). The response is consistently proportionate to the legitimacy of the object sought, not uniform in kind.

The human-to-God direction of seeking reveals a relationship of dependence and covenantal trust: the seeker approaches God as the source of guidance, deliverance, and life (Ps.34.4 'I sought the Lord, and he answered me and delivered me'; Amos.5.4 'Seek me and live'), showing the relationship is characterized by the human party's reliance on God's willingness to respond and God's reciprocal availability to be found (Isa.55.6 'while he may be found').

The superscription sets it after "he changed his behavior before Abimelech"; "When the humble see it they will be glad" (Psa 69:32). "It" is the deliverance of the speaker, who has said "I am afflicted and in pain" (69:29); I read: in both psalms, one man's boast is in the Lord, not in himself, and the humble are those who are glad at it. Their gladness is at what God did for someone else.

The vocabulary arc of shachar moves from an etymological base of 'early/dawn' to a general sense of diligent, eager seeking, applicable to both righteous devotion (seeking God, Ps.78.34) and illicit desire (Prov.7.15) -- showing the term's range is defined by intensity of pursuit rather than by the moral quality of the object sought.

In Ps.78.34, darash (H1875, same cluster) and M11/M81 (repented) co-occur with shachar; from shachar's own vantage the eager-intensity pursuit sits alongside darash's more general seeking as a rhetorical doubling (seeking...sought earnestly), while repentance remains the separate inward-turning act that darash's pass already covers.

H7836 (shachar) shares the subgroup's general 'intensive/earnest seeking' theme with G1567/G1934 conceptually (both Greek terms and shachar converge on devotional 'seek God/wisdom diligently' senses: shachar in Ps.63.1, Isa.26.9, Job.8.5, Prov.8.17, Ps.78.34 parallels ekzeteo in Acts.15.17/Heb.11.6/Rom.3.11 and epizeteo's aspirational uses), but there is no lexical or morphological relationship -- shachar is a distinct Hebrew root (tied etymologically to 'dawn/early') with no direct Greek cognate among this subgroup's members, and unlike ekzeteo/epizeteo it never carries a judicial 'demand an account/blood' sense; its 'demanding' pole (Job.7.21, God seeking Job) is ironic-reversal rather than legal exaction.

Shachar's occurrence in Prov.11.27 ('diligently seeks good...but evil comes to him who searches for it') stands alongside its cluster-sibling H1245 (baqash) within the very same verse, forming an intra-verse doublet of intensive-seeking terms -- this pairing (also seen with H1875 darash alongside shachar in Ps.78.34, and H1245 alongside shachar in Hos.5.15) shows the Hebrew seeking-vocabulary routinely stacks multiple intensive roots together for rhetorical emphasis, a stacking pattern not seen between the two Greek members (ekzeteo and epizeteo never co-occur in the same verse in this occurrence set).

Both patterns occur. In devotional occurrences the seeking follows a prior belief (Heb.11.6 -- one must first 'believe that he exists' before seeking him for reward), while in penitential occurrences (Hos.5.15, Ps.78.34) seeking follows judgment/distress and produces or confirms acknowledgment of guilt. In judicial occurrences (Luke.11.50-51) the 'seeking/requiring' itself constitutes the judgement (an act of holding accountable), so it does not precede a separate belief but enacts one.

Both are attested. Reversible: seeking that leads to finding and repentance (Prov.8.17, Ps.78.34) can be entered into or renewed. Irreversible: Esau's seeking in Heb.12.17 comes after a disqualifying act and 'he found no chance to repent' -- the door once closed cannot be reopened by any degree of subsequent earnest seeking, making that particular instance of the characteristic irreversible in its outcome though not in the seeking-act itself.

A recurring sequence: acknowledgment of guilt precedes seeking (Hos.5.15 'until they acknowledge their guilt and seek my face'); belief precedes seeking (Heb.11.6, 'must believe...and that he rewards those who seek him'); seeking precedes finding (Prov.8.17 'seek me diligently find me'); and being killed/judged precedes repentance which accompanies seeking (Ps.78.34 'When he killed them, they sought him; they repented').

Across the verses, the characteristic follows a belief more often than it precedes one: Heb.11.6 makes belief in God's existence and rewarding character the explicit precondition for seeking; Hos.5.15 and Ps.78.34 show acknowledgment of guilt/repentance preceding the earnest seeking. In the demanding-sign occurrences, however, the seeking itself reveals an already-formed unbelieving judgment (the generation is 'evil and adulterous') rather than producing a new belief -- so the characteristic mostly follows or expresses prior belief/disposition rather than generating one, with the sign-demanding cases showing seeking as an expression of settled unbelief rather than a step toward belief.

The consistent order is: acknowledgment/distress -> seeking -> repentance/finding.

Both belong to this subgroup's 'thoroughness or added directedness' core description, but each realizes a different half of it: ekzeteo leans toward thoroughness, epizeteo toward directedness/insistence.

The evidence shows both: Esau's forfeiture in Heb.12.17 is irreversible (his tearful seeking cannot undo the prior choice, 'no chance to repent'), and Israel's failure in Rom.11.7 leads to hardening presented as a settled state ('the rest were hardened'). But other cases show seeking leading to attainment and reversal of separation (Prov.8.17 'find me'; Hos.5.15 leads to God's return). The transformation's reversibility depends entirely on timing and divine response, not on the intensity of the seeking itself.
